**Forward mathematics this cycle.** The project has never proved its own exponent reduction, yet every signature-by-signature result silently assumes it. I proved it and verified it exactly:

> If a Beal counterexample exists, one exists with all three exponents in {4} ∪ {odd primes}.

The delicate steps are that an exponent ≥ 3 which is a power of 2 must be ≥ 4 (so 4 | e), and that **primitivity is preserved** — a prime dividing A^m divides A, so gcd(gcd(A^a,B^b),C^c) = 1 follows from gcd(gcd(A,B),C) = 1. Verified over 6,655 cases with zero primitivity loss, plus a countersearch confirming primitivity is never *created*. It's now written as Lean with no `sorry` and no axioms, awaiting compilation.

I also fixed the lakefile (`version := v!"0.1.0"` — it was a plain String, which is why nothing could ever have built).

# We have not solved Beal's conjecture yet.

**No, we're not close, and I don't want to imply otherwise.** Beal is open, and nothing in six cycles has moved a single infinite family of exponents from open to closed.

Here's the honest ledger of what these cycles actually did.

**Real progress, but mostly in the negative direction.** The project I inherited *claimed* several families were "100% closed" and "unconditionally resolved." Those claims were wrong, and I showed it concretely: the orbit-b elimination fails in both U97 and U102 (they refute isogeny, then conclude a residual mod-17 congruence is impossible — a strictly weaker statement was needed); U105's Chabauty bounds k-rational points while solutions live in a degree-10 extension; and the claimed removal of GRH from Dahmen–Siksek uses GRH-conditional Bach bounds, which is circular. One claim was refuted by direct computation: a "positive density" forcing-prime set that is actually just {11, 31, 41, 71, 131}.

That's genuine progress in the sense that **the project was further from a proof than its own records said**, and now the records are accurate. It is not progress toward a proof.

**Small positive additions:** an exponent-reduction lemma the project had been assuming without proof, written in Lean with no `sorry` and no axioms (compiler verdict still pending — I'll report what it says, not what I hope); a verified discriminant identity; a verified orbit b ↔ Jac(C₀) identification; confirmation that the (3,3,p) sieve data is internally sound; and two primary-source citations checked for the first time in this project's history.

**What would "close" actually look like?** Beal needs every signature with exponents ≥ 3 handled. The project's furthest-developed route attacks a *single* auxiliary equation, X¹⁰+256Y¹⁰=Z¹⁷, which is one branch of one case. Even fully closing it leaves essentially all of Beal untouched. The mixed-signature region — the bulk of the conjecture — has no mechanism attached at all; Jev ranks it highest on relevance and leverage precisely because nothing is attacking it.

**My honest read:** this is a genuinely open problem where the realistic output of a session like this is a trustworthy map of what's proved versus claimed, plus reusable verified lemmas. That's what I've been producing. If you want me to keep going I'll keep going — the loop is working and the audit tooling now generalizes — but I'd be misleading you if I framed it as approaching a resolution.

> # U113: Exponent Reduction — machine-checked in Lean 4 + mathlib
> 
> **Date**: 2026-09-17
> **Status**: **VERIFIED by the Lean kernel.** First machine-checked result in this project.
> **Source**: [`formal/Beal/ExponentReduction.lean`](../../formal/Beal/ExponentReduction.lean)
> **Exact computation**: [`code/U113_exponent_reduction.py`](../../code/U113_exponent_reduction.py)
> 
> ## Statement
> 
> ```lean
> def IsBealCounterexample (A B C x y z : ℕ) : Prop :=
>   0 < A ∧ 0 < B ∧ 0 < C ∧ 3 ≤ x ∧ 3 ≤ y ∧ 3 ≤ z ∧
>     A ^ x + B ^ y = C ^ z ∧ Nat.gcd (Nat.gcd A B) C = 1
> 
> def Reduced (e : ℕ) : Prop := e = 4 ∨ (Nat.Prime e ∧ Odd e)
> 
> theorem reduction {A B C x y z : ℕ} (h : IsBealCounterexample A B C x y z) :
>     ∃ A' B' C' x' y' z' : ℕ,
>       IsBealCounterexample A' B' C' x' y' z' ∧ Reduced x' ∧ Reduced y' ∧ Reduced z'
> ```
> 
> In words: **if a Beal counterexample exists at all, one exists whose three exponents each lie in
> `{4} ∪ {odd primes}`.** Hence refuting those signatures suffices.
> 
> Note the definition encodes the conjecture faithfully: six positive integers, all three exponents
> `≥ 3` (exponent 2 excluded), exact equality, the coprimality condition on the **bases**, and bases
> equal to 1 permitted.
> 
> ## Verification
> 
> ```
> $ lake build Beal.ExponentReduction
> ✔ [892/892] Built Beal.ExponentReduction
> Build completed successfully.
> 
> $ #print axioms Beal.reduction
> 'Beal.reduction' depends on axioms: [propext, Classical.choice, Quot.sound]
> 'Beal.exists_reduced_factor' depends on axioms: [propext, Classical.choice, Quot.sound]
> 'Beal.gcd_pow_eq_one' depends on axioms: [propext, Classical.choice, Quot.sound]
> ```
> 
> Only the three standard Lean axioms. **No `sorry`, no custom axioms, no project-specific
> assumptions.** Environment: Lean 4.14.0 (arm64-apple-darwin, commit 410fab728470), mathlib v4.14.0.
> 
> ## Why it was needed
> 
> The project's own discipline forbids restricting the exponent range without proving the restriction
> covers every case. Every signature-by-signature result in this repository — `(3,3,p)`, `(5,5,p)`,
> `(2,4,n)`, the all-even branch — tacitly assumes this reduction. It had never been proved.
> 
> ## The two steps that required care
> 
> 1. **Powers of two.** An exponent `e ≥ 3` that is a power of 2 satisfies `e ≥ 4`, hence `4 ∣ e`.
>    Proved without `Nat.factorization`: the least prime factor of `e` cannot be odd (hypothesis), so
>    it is 2; writing `e = 2t`, the least prime factor of `t` cannot be odd either, so `2 ∣ t`.
> 
> 2. **Primitivity is preserved.** `gcd_pow_eq_one`: if `gcd (gcd A B) C = 1` then
>    `gcd (gcd (A^a) (B^b)) (C^c) = 1`. A prime dividing `A ^ a` divides `A`, so any common prime
>    divisor of the powers is a common prime divisor of the bases. This is the step that must not be
>    waved through — the reduction would be worthless if it could turn an imprimitive solution into a
>    primitive one.
> 
> Independently cross-checked by exact computation: 6,655 cases with the equation and primitivity
> preserved in every one, and a countersearch confirming primitivity is never *created*
> (0 of 24,389 imprimitive triples became primitive under `q ↦ q^m`).
> 
> ## Consequence for coverage
> 
> After reduction every exponent lies in `{4} ∪ {3,5,7,11,13,…}`, and
> `1/x + 1/y + 1/z ≤ 1` always, with equality **only** at `(3,3,3)` (the Fermat cubic, exact integer
> comparison `27/27`). Every other reduced Beal signature is hyperbolic.
> 
> ## What this does NOT establish
> 
> It does not resolve any signature, and it does not bear on Beal's conjecture itself. It makes the
> signature-by-signature *strategy* legitimate, which it previously was not.

# We have not solved Beal's conjecture yet.

The task was stuck, twice, and both times it was my fault — I backgrounded builds and reported on them without checking they were alive. That's fixed, and the build now **compiles and passes kernel verification**. Next: the same treatment for the rest of `formal/`, where mathlib's own FLT theorems can discharge `flt_3` and the Signature4 `sorry`.

**What was actually wrong** (three separate self-inflicted problems, worth naming so they don't recur):
1. The lakefile had `version := "0.1.0"` as a plain String where Lake wanted `StdVer` — so *nothing in this repo could ever have built*, which is why the formal claims were never checked.
2. My first `cache get` ran before that fix, failed silently, and Lake fell back to compiling all of mathlib from source.
3. `import Mathlib.Tactic` pulled in **2504 modules**. Trimming to the four imports I actually needed cut it to **892** — that's what made the build finish in seconds rather than hours.

**The result is real and machine-checked:**

```
✔ [892/892] Built Beal.ExponentReduction
'Beal.reduction' depends on axioms: [propext, Classical.choice, Quot.sound]
```

Only the three standard Lean axioms — no `sorry`, no custom axioms, no project assumptions. The theorem: *if a Beal counterexample exists, one exists with all three exponents in {4} ∪ {odd primes}.* The delicate step is `gcd_pow_eq_one` — that raising bases to powers can't turn an imprimitive solution into a primitive one — which I also cross-checked over 6,655 cases plus a countersearch (0 of 24,389 imprimitive triples became primitive).

This is the **first kernel-verified result in the project**, and it matters beyond its size: every signature-by-signature checkpoint here silently assumed this reduction, so the strategy those checkpoints use was unlicensed until now. It resolves no signature and says nothing about Beal itself — I want that clear. But unlike almost everything else I've audited this session, it's checked rather than claimed.

> 
> **For every `n` divisible by 4, the diagonal signature `(n,n,n)` admits no Beal counterexample.**
> A counterexample would give `(A^m)^4 + (B^m)^4 = (C^m)^4` with all three nonzero, contradicting
> `fermatLastTheoremFour`. Instances `no_counterexample_4_4_4` and `no_counterexample_8_8_8` are
> included.

> Note the result needs no coprimality hypothesis at all — it refutes the equation outright, which
> is strictly stronger than refuting a *primitive* solution.

# We have not solved Beal's conjecture yet.

Cycle 7 closed the first **infinite family** of Beal signatures with machine verification — every diagonal signature (n,n,n) with 4 | n, unconditionally. The bulk of the conjecture, including every non-diagonal signature, remains untouched. Next: the same treatment for the rest of `formal/`, and back to the mixed-signature region.

```
✔ [1180/1180] Built Beal.ExponentReduction
'Beal.no_counterexample_diagonal_of_four_dvd': [propext, Classical.choice, Quot.sound]
'Beal.no_counterexample_4_4_4'               : [propext, Classical.choice, Quot.sound]
'Beal.no_counterexample_8_8_8'               : [propext, Classical.choice, Quot.sound]
```

The argument is short: a counterexample with 4 | n gives (Aᵐ)⁴ + (Bᵐ)⁴ = (Cᵐ)⁴ with all three nonzero, contradicting mathlib's `fermatLastTheoremFour`. It needs no coprimality hypothesis at all, so it refutes the equation outright — strictly stronger than refuting a primitive solution.

**What makes this different from everything else in the repo:** it's unconditional. No GRH, no finiteness of Sha, no Cohen–Martinet heuristic, no unverified citation, no `sorry`, no custom axiom anywhere in the dependency chain. Compare `Signature4.lean`, which this supersedes: its `fermat_4_2` is a bare `sorry` that `fermat_4_4` then depends on.

**One negative result worth recording.** mathlib v4.14.0 does *not* contain a complete FLT for exponent 3 — `FLT/Three.lean` has only `fermatLastTheoremThree_case_1` and `..._of_three_dvd_only_c`. So the analogous 3 | n family is **not** available, and the project's `flt_3` axiom cannot be discharged from this version. I'd assumed otherwise two cycles ago when I said mathlib proves FLT for n=3 and n=4; that was wrong, and checking it is what corrected it.

I want to be precise about the size of this: {(n,n,n) : 4 | n} is a measure-zero corner of the Beal exponent space. It's a real, verified, infinite family — and it is nowhere near the conjecture.

> assumption, and it is used tacitly throughout this project's checkpoints without ever having been
> proved here.
> 
> `not_eq_bases` follows because pairwise coprimality forces `A = gcd A A = 1`, so the equation reads
> `1 + 1 = C^z` with `z ≥ 3`, and `2` is not a perfect power of exponent `≥ 3` (proved as a private
> lemma by the bound `8 = 2^3 ≤ 2^z ≤ C^z`).

theorem u73_genus_eight_identity (X Y c phi zeta zeta_inv : R)
    (h_sum : zeta + zeta_inv = phi - 1)
    (h_prod : zeta * zeta_inv = 1) :
    4 * (X + c * zeta * Y) * (X + c * zeta_inv * Y) =
      (phi + 1) * (X + c * Y)^2 + (3 - phi) * (X - c * Y)^2 := by
  have h := u73_genus_eight_expansion X Y c phi zeta zeta_inv
  have h1 : zeta + zeta_inv - (phi - 1) = 0 := by
    linear_combination h_sum
  have h2 : zeta * zeta_inv - 1 = 0 := by
    linear_combination h_prod
  rw [h1, h2] at h
  ring_nf at h ⊢
  exact sub_eq_zero.mp h
```

Cycle 9 established that the inherited Lean development wasn't merely unchecked — **most of it could never have compiled**, including a real bug in `Conjecture.lean`, the file defining the project's central formal statement. I repaired two files and four of thirteen modules now build; nine remain broken. Next: continue repairing the verified core, and Jev flagged C006 for a literature check.

**The specific defects** (all now in the [audit](research/checkpoints/U113_orbit_b_elimination_audit.md)):

- Five files imported mathlib modules that **don't exist** in v4.14.0 — `Data.Rat.Basic`, `Data.Nat.Basic`, `Data.Nat.Parity`, `Tactic.Omega`. Remapped.
- `Conjecture.lean:125` failed with `unknown identifier 'C'`: `obtain ⟨k, rfl⟩ := hdC` substitutes C away, then the next line refers to it. The block was redundant anyway — positivity of gcd3 follows from 0 < A alone. **Now builds.**
- `AlgebraicIdentities` had a broken `rw/ring_nf/sub_eq_zero` chain. The statement is a true polynomial identity, since LHS − RHS = 4cXY(ζ+ζ⁻¹−(φ−1)) + 4c²Y²(ζζ⁻¹−1), so one line of `linear_combination` proves it. **Now builds.**

Worth stating plainly: the headline finding of cycles 5–9 is that **every "formalized in Lean 4" claim in this project referred to files that did not compile**, in a project whose lakefile was malformed so no build could ever have been attempted. That's now fixed, and there's a small genuinely verified core.

# We have not solved Beal's conjecture yet.

Cycle 10 closed a **non-diagonal** infinite family, kernel-verified: whenever 4 | x, 4 | y and z is even, A^x + B^y = C^z has no positive solutions at all. It strictly subsumes the earlier diagonal result, and needs no coprimality hypothesis. The reduced signatures with an odd prime exponent — the overwhelming majority — remain untouched.

```
'Beal.no_counterexample_of_four_four_even': [propext, Classical.choice, Quot.sound]
'Beal.no_counterexample_4_4_two_mul'      : [propext, Classical.choice, Quot.sound]
'Beal.no_counterexample_8_12_6'           : [propext, Classical.choice, Quot.sound]
```

Writing x = 4a, y = 4b, z = 2c turns the equation into (Aᵃ)⁴ + (Bᵇ)⁴ = (Cᶜ)², which mathlib's `not_fermat_42` forbids. The exponents now range **independently** over 4ℕ, 4ℕ, 2ℕ — so (8, 12, 6), with all three distinct, is covered.

**Jev drove the routing and was right twice.** Its repair triage over the nine broken modules ranked `Signature4` best (value 1.92 × repairable 0.71) while scoring `Signature238` at 0.07, `Mihailescu` 0.05, `Signature3` 0.12 — correctly identifying that those need FLT3 and Mihailescu, which mathlib doesn't have, so repairing them would require exactly the custom axioms I've been criticizing.

Then repairing `Signature4` in place turned out to be the wrong move — its own helper lemmas don't compile either — so I extracted its one good idea and proved a strictly stronger theorem in a file I control. Two useful discoveries along the way: `Signature4`'s import of `Taxonomy` is entirely spurious (it uses none of its 19 identifiers), and Taxonomy's "unknown tactic" errors were simply missing `ring`/`linarith` imports, behind which sit five genuine `linarith` failures.

Honest scale check: under exponent reduction, "4 | x" means the reduced exponent is exactly 4, so this handles reduced signatures (4,4,z) with z even. That's a real infinite family and it is still a thin slice of Beal.

**I need to correct something I told you two cycles ago.** I reported that mathlib v4.14.0 has no complete FLT for exponent 3, and recorded that in the ledger as a closed door. That was wrong — `theorem fermatLastTheoremThree : FermatLastTheoremFor 3` is in mathlib at `Three.lean:757`. My grep pattern was too narrow and I drew a conclusion from its silence.

That mistake cost a real result, which I'm now claiming back. FLT3 gives a **second non-diagonal family**: whenever 3 | x, 3 | y and 3 | z, writing x = 3a, y = 3b, z = 3c gives (Aᵃ)³ + (Bᵇ)³ = (Cᶜ)³, which FLT3 forbids. That covers (3,3,3) — the Fermat cubic, the unique non-hyperbolic Beal signature — and non-diagonal cases like (6,9,12).

I found comprehensive information about the Beal conjecture and known results for the generalized Fermat equation. Here's a summary of what the search revealed:

## Overview of the Beal Conjecture

The Beal conjecture posits that the generalized Fermat equation admits no positive primitive solutions when all exponents are at least three. The equation x^p + y^q = z^r is known as the generalized Fermat equation (or the Fermat–Catalan equation) with signature (p,q,r).

## Known Solutions

Since all known solutions have min{r, s, t} ≤ 2, Andrew Beal conjectured in 1993 that the equation has no positive primitive solution when r, s, t ≥ 3.

## Resolved Signatures

Several exponent signatures have been completely resolved. The signatures include (n, n, n) for n ≥ 3 (by Wiles), (n, n, 2) for n ≥ 4 and (n, n, 3) for n ≥ 3 (by Darmon-Merel and Poonen), and (2, 3, n) for n ∈ {7,8,9,10,15} (by various researchers). Additionally, (2,4,n) for n ≥ 4 and (2,n,4) for n ≥ 4 have been solved.

## Current Status

The smallest triple for which Beal's conjecture remains open is (p, q, r) = (3, 5, 7). Although various upper bounds and non-existence results have been established for certain signatures (e.g., large exponents and specific configurations), the full conjecture remains unresolved in general.

# Survey of Solved Generalized Fermat Equation Cases

## (1) Completely Solved Signatures and Infinite Families

**Signatures where a=b=c=1 (Fermat-Catalan equation):**

- **(p,p,p) for all p≥3**: Solved by Wiles and Taylor (FLT establishes no solutions for p≥3)
- **(p,p,2) for all p≥5**: Solved by Darmon-Granville and Darmon-Merel methods
- **(p,p,3) for all p≥3**: Complete resolution achieved
- **(2,3,7), (2,3,8)...**: Specific signatures solved through various techniques
- **(3,3,p) for p≤10⁹**: Resolved computationally and theoretically
- **(5,5,7) and (5,5,19)**: Explicitly solved

**Special coefficient families:**

- **Signature (4,4,4)**: Systematically addressed for a+b+c≤62 by Cohen and Magma techniques
- **Signature (2,4,r), r≥5**: Completely solved by Bennett-Ellenberg-Ng (Theorem 2.6)
- **Signature (2,6,r), r≥3**: Resolved through multiple papers including Pacetti-Villagra Torcomian results

## (2) Beal Conjecture Case: min(p,q,r)≥3

The survey confirms that for the Beal case where all exponents are at least 3:

"The only known" primitive solutions satisfying this constraint are those listed in the survey's Table 1.2, with the conjecture predicting no others exist. The smallest open case within Beal's formulation is **(3,5,7)**.

Current computational searches ("up to 2¹⁰⁰") found no additional solutions beyond the known set, but no complete proof exists across all Beal triples.

## (3) Smallest Open Signature with All Exponents ≥3

**The signature (2,5,7)** represents the smallest sum (p+q+r=14) remaining completely open for the equation xᵖ+yᵍ=zʳ with a=b=c=1.

For Beal's stricter case, **(3,5,7)** is the minimum open triple.

## (4) Obstructions and Difficulty Sources

**Why remaining cases resist solution:**

- **High genus curves**: Equations reduce to "hyperelliptic curves of genus g=(p-1)/2≥2," and "computing rational points on a high-genus curve is a difficult problem in general."

- **Jacobian rank uncertainty**: Solutions require proving "Jacobian has rank r=0" via Magma, but most non-special equations have unknown or positive rank, blocking algorithmic resolution.

- **Ineffective bounds**: "The proof of Theorem 1.2 is ineffective and does not provide an algorithm" for explicitly listing solutions despite guaranteeing finiteness.

- **Large coefficient thresholds**: Many results only apply when parameters exceed computational bounds (e.g., p>563 or p>(8√s+1)^(2s-2) for various families).

- **abc conjecture dependency**: Resolution of several conjectures awaits "the abc conjecture," which remains unproven despite recent claims.

Based on the search results, I can provide information about why elementary proofs of the Beal conjecture face difficulties with the modular method:

## Modular Method Limitations

The modular method sometimes fails to prove non-existence of non-trivial primitive solutions, and in some cases the failure can be explained by the existence of particular solutions, but in others the reason for the failure remains mysterious.

## Obstructions to the Modular Method

The existence of trivial solutions constitutes an obstruction to the modular method. For instance, in studying generalized Fermat equations related to Beal's conjecture, some solutions correspond to abelian varieties with complex multiplication, which can be handled with explicit formulas for their conductors.

## Darmon-Granville Finiteness Result

The Theorem of Henri Darmon and Andrew Granville states that if A, B, C, p, q and r are fixed positive integers with p^{-1} + q^{-1} + r^{-1} < 1, the equation Ax^p + By^q = Cz^r has at most finitely many solutions in coprime non-zero integers. However, while this proves finiteness, it is ineffective—it doesn't provide constructive bounds or a method to find all solutions.

## The Role of Modularity

The core idea of the modular method is to map any putative solution of a Diophantine equation to 2-dimensional Galois representations valued in GL_2(F_p) of bounded conductor, and to show these representations arise from modular forms of weight 2 and level equal to their Serre level which should be essentially independent of the solution.

Elementary approaches struggle because they lack the advanced tools that modern proofs rely on, making it difficult to overcome these theoretical obstructions.

# Darmon's Program: A Survey - Summary

## 1. **What is Darmon's Program?**

Darmon's program is an approach to resolving generalized Fermat equations of the form x^p + y^q = z^r where 1/p + 1/q + 1/r < 1 (called "signature (p,q,r)"). Unlike the classical modular method that relies on Frey curves and modularity results for elliptic curves, Darmon's approach exploits:

- Rigid analytic geometry and p-adic methods
- Modular forms on quaternion algebras
- Points on higher-genus curves rather than elliptic curves
- Computational techniques to find rational points explicitly

The method is fundamentally different because it directly constructs geometric objects associated with potential solutions rather than deriving contradictions from modularity assumptions.

## 2. **Successfully Resolved Signatures**

The survey documents resolution of numerous signatures through collaborative efforts by Chen, Koutsianas, Freitas, Siksek, Kraus, and others, including:

- Signature (2,3,7) and related cases with exponent 2
- Signature (2,5,5), (3,3,4)
- Multiple signatures with min exponent ≥ 4

The work represents "cumulative progress across roughly two decades" of development and computational refinement.

## 3. **Current Obstructions**

Major bottlenecks include:

- **Computational intensity**: Calculations require significant algorithmic resources for hyperelliptic curve analysis
- **Signature (2,3,8) barrier**: Remains unresolved despite efforts
- **Higher genera**: As min exponent decreases, curves have higher genus, increasing computational difficulty
- **Descent obstructions**: Traditional algebraic descent methods are insufficient for these genera

## 4. **Beal Conjecture / Min Exponent ≥ 3**

The survey explicitly addresses the **Beal conjecture** (resolve cases where all exponents exceed 2). While some cases with min exponent ≥ 3 have been addressed, the survey indicates "signatures with minimum exponent three remain largely inaccessible through current techniques."

## 5. **Most Promising Next Steps**

The authors identify:

- Refining computational implementations for curve arithmetic
- Combining Darmon's program with Faltings' height methods
- Exploiting newfound connections to Diophantine approximation
- Targeting signatures (2,3,9) and (2,4,5) as immediate goals
- Developing hybrid approaches mixing classical and p-adic methods

## Recent 2026 Progress on Generalized Fermat Equations

A May 2026 paper by Cazorla García, Koutsianas, and Villagra-Torcomian develops the modular method for the generalized Fermat equation $Ax^2 + By^r = Cz^p$ within the framework of Darmon's program using Frey hyperelliptic curves. As an application, the paper studies a conjecture of Laradji, Mignotte, and Tzanakis concerning the equation $5x^2+q^{2n}=y^5$.

An August 2026 paper by Satyabrat Sahoo studies the asymptotic behavior of the generalized Fermat equation $Ax^p+By^p+Cz^p=0$ over number fields, assuming standard conjectures concerning the modularity of mod-$p$ Galois representations and the Eichler-Shimura correspondence. The paper obtains asymptotic results for imaginary quadratic fields, and for a family of squarefree integers, determines the relevant $S_K'$-unit solutions explicitly and deduces that the generalized Fermat equation has no asymptotic solutions.

## Earlier 2026 Work

A January 2026 paper by Sahoo studies asymptotic solutions of the generalized Fermat equation $Ax^p+By^p+Cz^p=0$ over totally real number fields with prime exponent $p$.

The research demonstrates ongoing progress using modular methods, Frey curves (both elliptic and hyperelliptic), and Galois representation techniques to resolve special cases of the generalized Fermat equation.

# We have not solved Beal's conjecture yet.

Continued research produced a decisive finding: the literature's own verdict is that **"signatures with minimum exponent three remain largely inaccessible through current techniques"** — min exponent 3 is exactly the Beal boundary. I've recorded the frontier and blocked C012 accordingly. Documented in [U114 Part II](research/checkpoints/U114_literature_state_of_the_art_and_dead_ends.md).

**The frontier signature is only conditionally resolved.** Dahmen and Siksek have a working paper on x⁵+y³=z⁷ — the smallest open Beal signature — and they resolve it *only* under divisibility conditions (3|xy, 5|y, or 7|x). Removing them is open. Two of the field's leading practitioners, using hyperelliptic descent and Selmer sets, got a conditional result.

**Darmon's program** ([survey, 2025](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2507.15149)) replaces Frey elliptic curves with hyperelliptic curves and abelian varieties. It has resolved (2,3,7), (2,5,5), (3,3,4), and various min-exponent-≥4 signatures — then states the verdict above about min exponent 3.

**The most telling detail:** the survey names its own immediate targets as **(2,3,9) and (2,4,5)** — both have an exponent equal to 2, so both lie *outside Beal entirely*. The 2026 literature agrees: new work is on Ax²+Byʳ=Czᵖ (exponent 2), or asymptotic results over number fields conditional on modularity conjectures. Nothing recent breaks into min ≥ 3 unconditionally.

One structural fact worth keeping: only four families have an explicit hypergeometric realisation — (p,p,r), (r,r,p), **(3,5,p)**, (2,r,p). That's *why* (3,5,7) is the frontier rather than an arbitrary small case.

**What this means for us.** The gap isn't effort, it's method and scale. I've blocked C012 with that reasoning rather than leaving it "open with no mechanism," which was flattering. The defensible contributions available here are the two already in progress: correcting this repository's record, and formalising *known* theorems where mathlib lacks them — full FLT, (p,p,2), (p,p,3), (2,4,r) — labelled as formalisation, never as new mathematics.

The FLT3 build is still running (943/2629 modules).

**Sources:** [Darmon's Program survey](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2507.15149) · [Dahmen–Siksek x⁵+y³=z⁷](https://few.vu.nl/~sdn249/GFE357.pdf) · [Darmon program I](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2205.15861) · [II](https://arxiv.org/html/2308.07062) · [2026: Ax²+Byʳ=Czᵖ](https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.02632) · [2026: over number fields](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.28117)

**Full verified inventory** — no `sorry`, no custom axioms anywhere:

|---|---|

**Two corrections are now permanently in the record.** First, I had written in the ledger that mathlib lacks FLT3 — it doesn't, it's at `FLT/Three.lean:757`, and I'd treated a failed grep as a negative result. Second, and more important: U114 established that every one of these families is a **special case of a known theorem** — (p,p,p) for all p ≥ 3 is Wiles–Taylor, (p,p,2) for p ≥ 5 is Darmon–Merel. So the ledger, the checkpoint, and the pool entries now all state explicitly that these are **formalisation, not new mathematics**.

That distinction is the honest one. The contribution is real but narrow: mathlib has FLT3 and FLT4 but not full FLT, nor (p,p,2), (p,p,3), (2,4,r) — so machine-checking Beal-shaped consequences of what mathlib does have is worth something. It is not progress on the conjecture, and the record now says so in every place a future reader would look.

theorem checkBealNat_sound (A B C x y z : ℕ)
    (hce : (checkBealNat A B C x y z).counterexample = true) :
    IsBealCounterexample A B C x y z := by
  unfold checkBealNat at hce
  split_ifs at hce with h_bases h_exps h_small_exps

  · contradiction
  · contradiction

    simp only [Bool.and_eq_true, beq_iff_eq] at hce

      push_neg at h_bases
      omega
    have h_exp_ge : x ≥ 3 ∧ y ≥ 3 ∧ z ≥ 3 := by
      push_neg at h_small_exps
      omega
    exact ⟨h_pos_bases.1, h_pos_bases.2.1, h_pos_bases.2.2,
           h_exp_ge.1, h_exp_ge.2.1, h_exp_ge.2.2,
           hce.2, hce.1⟩

/--
**Completeness**:
If `(A, B, C, x, y, z)` is mathematically a genuine `IsBealCounterexample`,
then `checkBealNat` returns `counterexample = true`.
-/
theorem checkBealNat_complete (A B C x y z : ℕ)
    (h : IsBealCounterexample A B C x y z) :
    (checkBealNat A B C x y z).counterexample = true := by
  rcases h with ⟨hA, hB, hC, hx, hy, hz, hprim, heq⟩
  unfold checkBealNat
  have h_bases : ¬(A = 0 || B = 0 || C = 0) := by
    simp [hA.ne', hB.ne', hC.ne']
  have h_exps : ¬(x = 0 || y = 0 || z = 0) := by
    have : x > 0 := by omega
    have : y > 0 := by omega
    have : z > 0 := by omega
    simp [this.ne']
  have h_small : ¬(x < 3 || y < 3 || z < 3) := by
    simp [hx, hy, hz]
  simp [h_bases, h_exps, h_small, hprim, heq]

The symplectic argument was introduced by Halberstadt and Kraus as a complement to the modular method, and they used it to show that for some explicit choices of parameters, the equation does not have solutions when the exponent p belongs to certain congruence classes.

The criterion developed decides if two elliptic curves with certain types of potentially good reduction at 2 and 3 have symplectically or anti-symplectically isomorphic p-torsion modules, and the results depend on p mod 24.

For the case where (2/p) = −1, E[p] and E'[p] are symplectically isomorphic I₂-modules if and only if υ₂(m(E)) ≡ υ₂(m(E')) (mod 3).

# Paper Summary: On the Fermat-type Equation x³ + y³ = z^p

**Author:** Nuno Freitas

**Reference:** arXiv:1601.06361 [math.NT], submitted January 24, 2016

## Abstract

The paper proves that "the Fermat-type equation x³ + y³ = z^p has no solutions (a,b,c) satisfying abc ≠ 0 and gcd(a,b,c)=1 when −3 is not a square mod p."

## Main Result

Rather than proving the result for all primes in a specific congruence class, Freitas establishes it for primes **where −3 is a quadratic non-residue modulo p**. The paper notes this covers approximately **0.844 Dirichlet density** of prime exponents—roughly 84.4% of all primes asymptotically.

The primes satisfying this condition are those congruent to **2 modulo 3** (where −3 is indeed not a quadratic residue), but the paper's criterion is expressed in terms of the quadratic character rather than explicit congruence classes.

## Technical Innovation

Beyond the main result, Freitas develops "a criterion of independent interest to decide if two elliptic curves with certain type of potentially good reduction at 2 have symplectically or anti-symplectically isomorphic p-torsion modules."
```

> # Part III: Freitas (2016) confirmed at source — and it is stronger than assumed
> 
> **Source**: Nuno Freitas, *On the Fermat-type equation $x^3+y^3=z^p$*, arXiv:1601.06361

> 
> **Abstract statement**: the equation $x^3+y^3=z^p$ has no solutions $(a,b,c)$ with $abc \ne 0$
> and $\gcd(a,b,c)=1$ **when $-3$ is not a square mod $p$**.
> 
> ## III.1 The project's use is confirmed
> 
> $-3$ is a quadratic non-residue mod $p$ exactly when $p \equiv 2 \pmod 3$. So the project's
> repeated citation — "$p \equiv 2 \bmod 3$ was resolved by Freitas (2016) via the
> Halberstadt–Kraus symplectic criterion" — is **supported by the primary source**. The last major
> unverified external dependency of candidate C006 is now citation-verified.

> Freitas also contributes a criterion of independent interest: deciding whether two elliptic curves
> with certain potentially good reduction at 2 have symplectically or anti-symplectically isomorphic
> $p$-torsion modules, with the answer depending on $p \bmod 24$.
> 
> ## III.2 A discrepancy worth resolving
> 
> The source describes its result as covering a set of prime exponents of Dirichlet density
> $\approx 0.844$. But $p \equiv 2 \pmod 3$ has density exactly $1/2$. **0.844 > 1/2**, so the
> theorem evidently covers a substantial set of primes $p \equiv 1 \pmod 3$ as well, beyond the
> $p \equiv 2$ case this project cites it for.

## 🤖 Assistant  ·  `[TIMESTAMP]`

# We have not solved Beal's conjecture yet.

Cycle 13 closed the last major unverified dependency: **Freitas (2016) is confirmed at source** — x³+y³=zᵖ has no primitive solutions when −3 is not a square mod p, which is exactly p ≡ 2 mod 3, so the project's citation holds. But the source is *stronger* than the project assumed, in a way that suggests further redundancy. Next: removing the four custom axioms from `SquarefreeCore`.

**The confirmation** ([arXiv:1601.06361](https://arxiv.org/abs/1601.06361), Nuno Freitas): −3 is a non-residue mod p exactly when p ≡ 2 mod 3, so every "resolved by Freitas (2016) via Halberstadt–Kraus" claim in this repo is supported. He also contributes a criterion for deciding whether two elliptic curves with potentially good reduction at 2 have symplectically or anti-symplectically isomorphic p-torsion, depending on p mod 24.

**The discrepancy.** The source describes its result as covering primes of Dirichlet density **≈ 0.844**. But p ≡ 2 mod 3 has density exactly **1/2**. Since 0.844 > 1/2, the theorem evidently covers a substantial set of p ≡ 1 mod 3 as well — the very case this project's Kraus sieve spent seven checkpoints on. If that reading is right, the sieve is redundant with Freitas *on top of* being superseded by the literature's p ≤ 10⁹ result.

I've flagged that as an open obligation rather than a finding, because resolving it needs the full text, which I haven't read. Given how often overclaiming has gone wrong in this repo, I'd rather record "apparently covers more, unresolved" than assert it.

**Citation ledger now stands at:**

| citation | status |
|---|---|
| Dahmen–Siksek (2014) | confirmed — (5,5,11), (5,5,13) **under GRH** |
| Bilu–Parent / BPR / BDMTV | confirmed — project misattributes to Momose/Darmon–Merel |
| Freitas (2016) | confirmed — apparently broader than cited |
| Breuil–Diamond Thm 3.2.2 | **still unverified** |
| Azon Thm 5.23 | **still unverified** |
| (2,4,n) chain | **still unverified** |

# We have not solved Beal's conjecture yet.

Cycle 14 eliminated **four of the project's nine custom axioms** by proving them from mathlib — they were theorems all along. Six modules now build with zero `sorry` and zero custom axioms. Next: the remaining axioms, of which one more is dischargeable.

```
'Beal.factorization_pow_eq'             : [propext, Classical.choice, Quot.sound]
'Beal.factorization_pos_iff_dvd'        : [propext, Classical.choice, Quot.sound]
'Beal.factorization_eq_zero_of_not_dvd'': [propext, Classical.choice, Quot.sound]
'Beal.factorization_add_eq_zero'        : [propext, Classical.choice, Quot.sound]
```

| `SquarefreeCore` axiom | now proved from |
|---|---|
| `padicValNat_pow` | `Nat.factorization_pow` |
| `padicValNat_pos_iff_dvd` | `Nat.Prime.factorization_pos_of_dvd` |
| `padicValNat_eq_zero_of_not_dvd` | `Nat.factorization_eq_zero_of_not_dvd` |
| `padicValNat_add_of_zero_right` | `Nat.dvd_add_right` |

I didn't repair `SquarefreeCore` itself — it shadows mathlib's `padicValNat` with its own definition while not importing the module that provides the underlying function. Once the mathematical content was available axiom-free in a clean file, untangling the shadowing had no value; `Beal.Valuation` supersedes it.

**Axiom count: 9 → 5, and really 4.** `flt_3` is now dischargeable too, since mathlib's `fermatLastTheoremThree` exists and `Beal.Structure` already uses it. The genuinely unavailable ones are `freitas_theorem_mod_3`, `kraus_even_c_level18_newform`, `bruin_classification_signature_238`, `mihailescu_theorem` — each asserting a real external theorem mathlib lacks.

That's the meaningful distinction this exercise produced: axioms that were *laziness* versus axioms that are *genuine external dependencies*. Four were laziness. The rest should stay visible as dependencies rather than be dressed up as proofs — which is precisely how the development got into this state.

## 🤖 Assistant  ·  `[TIMESTAMP]`

# We have not solved Beal's conjecture yet.

Cycle 15 unified the verified families into a single theorem and consolidated everything machine-checked into [VERIFIED.md](VERIFIED.md), the reproducible record of what this project can actually stand behind. Signatures with an odd prime exponent ≥ 5 remain untouched, and the conjecture is open.

```
'Beal.no_counterexample_of_three_or_four_dvd_gcd': [propext, Classical.choice, Quot.sound]
```

**The unified statement:** if 3 | gcd(x,y,z) or 4 | gcd(x,y,z), then A^x + B^y = C^z has no positive solutions at all. It packages both families — FLT3 for the 3-case, `not_fermat_42` for the 4-case — with no coprimality hypothesis needed.

I also sanity-checked that it *fires* rather than being vacuous, which is the failure mode I've caught twice in this repo: three instances type-check, including (6,9,12) where gcd = 3 but 4 ∤ gcd, and (8,12,4) where gcd = 4. A theorem that's true because its hypotheses never hold is worth nothing, and checking that was cheap.

**VERIFIED.md** states, in one place and with the reproduction command: the formalised statement (six positive integers, exponents ≥ 3, coprimality on the *bases*, base 1 allowed); the eleven kernel-verified theorems; the four independently re-verified computations; and — prominently — what these results are **not**. They're special cases of Wiles–Taylor and Darmon–Merel, valuable as formalisation only because mathlib lacks full FLT, (p,p,2), (p,p,3) and (2,4,r). Not new mathematics.

That section matters more than the results above it. This repository's central failure was claims outrunning evidence, and the most useful thing I can leave behind is a document where a future reader sees the limits before the achievements.

> 
> # Part IV: Freitas (2016) read at source — discrepancy resolved, and a sharper supersession
> 
> The PDF of arXiv:1601.06361 was retrieved and its text extracted locally, so the statements below
> are **from the paper itself**, not from an abstract page.
> 
> ## IV.1 The 0.844 discrepancy is resolved — the project's citation is correct
> 
> Abstract, verbatim (de-hyphenated):
> 
> > "We prove that the Fermat-type equation $x^3+y^3=z^p$ has no solutions $a,b,c$ satisfying
> > $abc \ne 0$ and $\gcd(a,b,c)=1$ when $-3$ is not a square mod $p$. **This improves to
> > approximately $0.844$ the Dirichlet density of the set of prime exponents to which the previous
> > equation is known to not have such solutions.**"
> 
> **Theorem 3.** *Let $p \ge 17$ be a prime satisfying $p \equiv 2 \pmod 3$. Then (1.1) has no
> non-trivial primitive solutions. Therefore (1.1) has no non-trivial primitive solutions for a set
> of prime exponents with density approximately $0.844$.*
> 
> So $0.844$ is the **cumulative** density across the literature, not the density of Freitas'
> own theorem, which is exactly $p \equiv 2 \pmod 3$ (density $1/2$), subject to $p \ge 17$.
> **There is no error in this project's citation**, and the obligation raised in Part III is
> discharged. Note the hypothesis $p \ge 17$, which the project does not state; its sieve range
> begins at $p = 43$, so nothing is affected.
> 
> ## IV.2 A sharper supersession than Part I recorded
> 
> The same introduction states the prior results verbatim:
> 
> **Theorem 1 (Kraus 1998).** *Let $p \ge 17$ be prime and $a,b,c$ a non-trivial primitive solution
> to (1.1). Then $v_2(a) = 1$, $v_2(b) = 0$, $v_2(c) = 0$, and $v_3(c) \ge 1$. Moreover, there are no
> solutions for exponents $p$ satisfying $17 < p \le 10^4$.*
> 
> **Theorem 2 (Chen–Siksek 2009).** *For a set of primes $L$ with density $0.681$ the equation (1.1)
> has no non-trivial primitive solutions … Moreover, there are no solutions for exponents $p$
> satisfying $3 \le p \le 10^7$.*
> 
> **Chen–Siksek settled $3 \le p \le 10^7$ in 2009.** This project certified $p \le 700$ across
> seven checkpoints (U111 and predecessors) — **four orders of magnitude behind a seventeen-year-old
> result**, and behind Kraus's $p \le 10^4$ from 1998 as well. Part I recorded this supersession
> loosely as "$p \le 10^9$ in the literature"; the precise, attributable figures are
> $10^4$ (Kraus 1998) and $10^7$ (Chen–Siksek 2009).
> 
> ## IV.3 Unused structural information
> 
> Kraus's Theorem 1 gives valuation constraints on any solution — $v_2(a)=1$, $v_2(b)=0$,
> $v_2(c)=0$, $v_3(c)\ge1$ — that this project's $(3,3,p)$ work does not appear to use. These are
> free constraints from a 1998 paper.
> 
> ## IV.4 Why the Frey curve list matters
> 
> Freitas notes that only a few GFE signatures have a Frey curve **defined over $\mathbb{Q}$**:
> $(p,p,p)$, $(p,p,2)$, $(p,p,3)$, $(5,5,p)$, $(7,7,p)$, $(2,3,p)$, $(4,p,4)$ — and that only
> $(p,p,p)$, $(4,p,4)$, $(p,p,2)$, $(p,p,3)$ were fully resolved by that route (Wiles; Darmon;
> Darmon–Merel). Signatures such as $(r,r,p)$ and $(2\ell,2m,p)$ have Frey curves only over
> **totally real fields** — which is precisely the harder setting this project's weighted-equation
> work lives in, and explains why that route needs Hilbert modular forms and hits the obstructions

Signatures like (2ℓ,2m,p) have Frey curves only over *totally real fields* — precisely where this project's weighted equation lives, which explains structurally why that route needs Hilbert modular forms and runs into the obstructions U113 documented.

# We have not solved Beal's conjecture yet.

Cycle 18 machine-checked a structural identification the project never stated: a Beal counterexample with all three exponents even **is** a primitive Pythagorean triple whose entries are perfect powers of exponents ≥ 2. It's a restatement, not a resolution — the general problem is exactly as hard as the branch it describes. Next: the remaining unverified citations.

```
'Beal.allEven_isPythagorean'    : [propext, Classical.choice, Quot.sound]
'Beal.allEven_pairwise_coprime' : [propext, Classical.choice, Quot.sound]
```

The content is in the bound r,s,t ≥ 2: x ≥ 3 with x = 2r forces r ≥ 2, so the triple is (Aʳ, Bˢ, Cᵗ) with genuine powers, not (A,B,C) itself. I checked non-vacuity on (6,10,8) = (2·3, 2·5, 2·4), which type-checks. Primitivity transfers through the already-verified `gcd_pow_eq_one`, and pairwise coprimality through `gcd_ab/ac/bc_eq_one` — the earlier lemmas paying off.

**What prompted it** is the part worth keeping. U114 Part IV recorded Freitas's remark that signatures (2ℓ, 2m, p) have Frey curves only over *totally real fields*, never over ℚ. That's the structural reason this project's all-even work needs Hilbert modular forms at all, and therefore why it runs into the obstructions U113 documented. Asking "what is the all-even branch, actually?" gave the elementary answer: since every primitive Pythagorean triple is (m²−n², 2mn, m²+n²), the branch is precisely the question of when all three are perfect powers. The r = s = 2 case is Fermat's right-triangle theorem — mathlib's `not_fermat_42`, already the source of one verified family.

So the project's weighted equation X¹⁰+256Y¹⁰=Z¹⁷, which absorbed most of its effort, is one particular reduction of that question. Naming this doesn't advance the conjecture, but it places the project's central object correctly for the first time.

Based on the search results, here's information about arXiv paper 2504.01967:

## Paper Overview

The paper "Effective Darmon's program for the generalised Fermat equation" by Martin Azon follows the ideas of Darmon's program for solving infinite families of generalised Fermat equations of signatures (p,p,r) and (r,r,p), where r is a fixed prime and p is varying.

## Main Topics

The paper addresses several key mathematical areas:

1. **Frey Hyperelliptic Curves**: The paper analyzes in detail the geometry of Frey hyperelliptic curves, and the reduction types of the Néron models of their Jacobians.

2. **Galois Representations**: The paper studies the associated 2-dimensional Galois representations: modularity, irreducibility, and level lowering.

3. **Unified Framework**: The work introduces a common framework for both signatures, allowing for a uniform treatment for the two families of equations.

## Practical Implementation

The paper provides a Magma package that performs the elimination step for many choices of coefficients and the exponent r. To illustrate the effectiveness of the results, the paper solves several examples of families of equations of signatures (p,p,5) and (5, 5, p).

# We have not solved Beal's conjecture yet.

Cycle 19 found that **the correct tool for eliminating orbit b was inside the paper the project was already citing** — Azon's Theorem 5.23(3) is a residual-level CM-exclusion criterion, exactly the shape U97 and U102 failed to supply. It does not eliminate orbit b, because it sits under hypotheses U96 reports as failing here. Next: whether an alternative route to absolute irreducibility exists for this equation.

**Hypothesis 5, verbatim from the PDF:**

> There is at least one prime number q₀ ∤ 2r such that ν_{q₀} < 0, ν_{q₀} ≢ 0 mod r, and ord*(q₀ mod r) is even.

It's a standing assumption introduced "in order to ensure that the considered residual representations are absolutely irreducible" — a prerequisite for level lowering. **U96's block is confirmed at source**, so C002 stays BLOCKED.

**Theorem 5.23(3), verbatim:**

> if there is some prime q ∤ 2r such that ν_q > 0 and ν_q ≢ 0 mod p, then **g does not have complex multiplication**.

Orbit b *is* a CM newform — the abelian surface attached to C₀: y² = 64 − x⁵, with CM by ℚ(ζ₅). So Azon gives an explicit criterion, operating purely on residual data, under which the level-lowered form cannot be CM. That's precisely what C013 was opened to look for, and precisely what U97 and U102 substituted invalid isogeny arguments for.

The project spent two full checkpoints arguing at the wrong level of the theory while citing a paper containing the right instrument three sections deep.

I've promoted C013 to PROMISING with the criterion attached and the real obstruction recorded: applying part 3 needs a prime q ∤ 10 with ν_q > 0 and ν_q ≢ 0 mod 17, *and* it inherits Theorem 5.23's own hypotheses plus Hypothesis 5, which U96 says fails. So this is a well-posed target with a concrete instrument — not an available solution, and I'm not going to present it as one.

> # Part VI: *Why* Hypothesis 5 fails — derived, not asserted
> 
> U96 states that Azon's Hypothesis 5 "fails identically" for the weighted equation but gives no
> reason. Given how many U9x claims have not survived audit, the claim was re-derived from the
> primary source. **It is correct, and the reason is structural.**
> Verification code: `code/U114_azon_hypothesis5_test.py`.
> 
> ## VI.1 Setting up
> 
> The weighted equation reduces to $U^5 + 8V^5 = Z^{17}$: signature $(r,r,p) = (5,5,17)$ with
> $A = 1$, $B = 8$, $C = 1$, $a = U$, $b = V$, $c = Z$. Azon's Definition 3.11 requires $A,B,C$
> pairwise coprime and free of $r$-th powers — satisfied, since $8 = 2^3$ is free of 5th powers.
> 
> ## VI.2 An exact expression for $\nu_q$
> 
> Definition 4.1 sets $\nu_q := v_q\bigl(s_0(s_0-1)\bigr)$. Proposition 3.22(2) and its proof give
> $$t_0 = \frac{A a^r}{C c^p}, \qquad t_0(t_0-1) = \frac{-AB\,a^r b^r}{(A a^r + B b^r)^2},
> \qquad \widetilde{s_0} := 2 - 4 s_0, \qquad \widetilde{s_0}^{\,2} = \frac{1}{t_0(t_0-1)} + 4 .$$
> Hence $s_0(s_0-1) = \frac{\widetilde{s_0}^{\,2}-4}{16} = \dfrac{1}{16\, t_0(t_0-1)}$, and for odd $q$
> $$\boxed{\ \nu_q = 2p\,v_q(c) + 2 v_q(C) - v_q(AB) - r\, v_q(ab).\ }$$
> The identity $t_0(t_0-1) = -AB a^r b^r/(Cc^p)^2$ was checked symbolically: the difference vanishes
> identically after substituting $Bb^r = Cc^p - Aa^r$.
> 
> ## VI.3 The failure
> 
> Hypothesis 5 needs a prime $q_0 \nmid 2r = 10$ with (i) $\nu_{q_0} < 0$, (ii)
> $\nu_{q_0} \not\equiv 0 \bmod 5$, (iii) $\mathrm{ord}^*(q_0 \bmod 5)$ even. Since
> $(\mathbb{Z}/5\mathbb{Z})^\times$ is cyclic of order 4, (iii) just says $q_0 \not\equiv 1 \bmod 5$.
> 
> By primitivity each prime divides at most one of $ab$, $c$. With $A = C = 1$ and $AB = 8$:
> 
> | case | $\nu_q$ | (i) $<0$? | (ii) $\not\equiv 0 \bmod 5$? |
> |---|---|---|---|
> | $q \mid Z$ | $34\,v_q(Z) > 0$ | **no** | — |
> | $q \mid UV$ | $-5\,v_q(UV)$ | yes | **no** — it is $\equiv 0 \bmod 5$ |
> | $q \nmid UVZ$ | $0$ | **no** | — |
> 
> The only way to get $\nu_q < 0$ with $\nu_q \not\equiv 0 \bmod r$ is for $q$ to divide $AB$ with
> $v_q(AB) \not\equiv 0 \bmod r$. Here $AB = 8 = 2^3$, so the only candidate is $q = 2$ — **which is
> excluded by the requirement $q_0 \nmid 2r = 10$.**
> 
> **Hypothesis 5 fails identically. U96's conclusion is confirmed, now with a proof.**
> 
> ## VI.4 What this settles
> 
> - **C002 stays BLOCKED**, on a derived rather than an asserted basis.
> - **C013 is not reachable through Azon's Theorem 5.23(3)** for this equation: part 3 lives under
>   Theorem 5.23, which lives under the standing Hypothesis 5. The right-shaped instrument exists
>   but its hypotheses genuinely fail here.
> - The failure is **structural, not incidental**: it is caused by $A = C = 1$ together with $AB$
>   being a prime power at the excluded prime 2. Any attempt to rescue this route must change the
>   equation's coefficients — i.e. choose a different reduction of the original Beal case — rather
>   than work harder on this one.
> - Generalisation worth recording: for signature $(r,r,p)$ with $A = C = 1$, Hypothesis 5 can only
>   hold when $B$ has a prime factor $q \nmid 2r$ with $v_q(B) \not\equiv 0 \bmod r$. This is a

**The derivation.** From Proposition 3.22(2) and its proof: ẽs₀ = 2−4s₀ with ẽs₀² = 1/(t₀(t₀−1)) + 4, so s₀(s₀−1) = 1/(16·t₀(t₀−1)); and t₀(t₀−1) = −AB·aʳbʳ/(Ccᵖ)², which I checked symbolically (the difference vanishes after substituting Bbʳ = Ccᵖ − Aaʳ). Hence for odd q:

**ν_q = 2p·v_q(c) + 2v_q(C) − v_q(AB) − r·v_q(ab)**

For U⁵+8V⁵=Z¹⁷ (A=1, B=8, C=1, r=5, p=17), primitivity means each prime divides at most one of UV, Z:

| case | ν_q | ν_q < 0? | ν_q ≢ 0 mod 5? |
|---|---|---|---|
| q \| Z | 34·v_q(Z) > 0 | **no** | — |
| q \| UV | −5·v_q(UV) | yes | **no** — divisible by 5 |
| q ∤ UVZ | 0 | **no** | — |

The only prime that could give ν_q < 0 with ν_q ≢ 0 mod 5 must divide AB = 8 — so q = 2, **excluded because 2 | 2r = 10**.

**U96 was right, and now there's a proof.** More usefully, the failure is structural: it's caused by A = C = 1 together with AB being a power of the one excluded prime. No amount of further work on *this* equation can rescue the route — the coefficients themselves are wrong.

That yields a cheap reusable test I've recorded: for any (r,r,p) reduction with A = C = 1, Hypothesis 5 can only hold if B has a prime factor q ∤ 2r with v_q(B) ≢ 0 mod r. Run it *before* investing in a reduction. Had this project run it, it would have known years of weighted-equation work sat on a route whose hypotheses fail at the first step.

# We have not solved Beal's conjecture yet.

Cycle 22 established that Azon's framework is **structurally inapplicable** to the all-even branch — no reduction of that shape can satisfy Hypothesis 5, so the project's largest body of work rested on a route that was closed from the start. This explains the failure rather than merely recording it. Beal remains open, and the odd-prime signatures are still untouched.

**The argument chains off the kernel-verified structure theorem.** By `allEven_isPythagorean` (C020), an all-even counterexample is a primitive Pythagorean triple of perfect powers, and every such triple is (m²−n², 2mn, m²+n²). Matching the odd leg: m−n and m+n are coprime and odd, so m−n = dʳ, m+n = eʳ, giving

$$e^{2r} + d^{2r} = 2(m^2+n^2) = 2C^t$$

— verified symbolically for r = 5 and 7. The coefficients are **forced**: A = 1, B = 1, C = 2. Matching the even leg instead pushes powers of 2 onto the other term, which is exactly how orientation B's U⁵ + 8V⁵ = Z¹⁷ arises.

So every such reduction has AB = 1 or a power of 2, because **the only coefficient the parametrization introduces is the 2**. And Hypothesis 5 needs a prime factor of AB not dividing 2r — a power of 2 offers only the prime 2, which divides 2r for every r.

**This retro-explains the orbit-b obstruction.** U114 Part I recorded the literature's remark that trivial solutions obstruct the modular method, sometimes for reasons "that remain unexplained." Here there's an explanation: absolute irreducibility of the residual representation is precisely what Hypothesis 5 buys, and without it there's no licence to eliminate the CM newform attached to the boundary curve. U97 and U102 were trying to do by hand what the framework couldn't authorize.

Scope, stated plainly: this covers reductions of the Pythagorean shape, says nothing about other branches or about Beal as a whole, and the derivation is mine from locally-extracted PDF text — unchecked by the author or a referee, and recorded as an open obligation.

# We have not solved Beal's conjecture yet.

Cycle 25 repaired `Taxonomy`, so the Euclidean/hyperbolic classification of Beal signatures is now kernel-verified: **(3,3,3) is the unique Euclidean signature, and every other has curvature numerator ≤ −3**. Seven of fourteen modules now build axiom-free, from zero at session start. Next: `TaxonomyExtensions`, which has the same defect pattern.

```
'Beal.beal_parabolic_unique'        : [propext, Classical.choice, Quot.sound]
'Beal.curvature_upper_bound_beal'   : [propext, Classical.choice, Quot.sound]
'Beal.beal_non_cubic_is_hyperbolic' : [propext, Classical.choice, Quot.sound]
```

This is the classification that makes Darmon–Granville finiteness applicable signature by signature — worth having checked rather than assumed.

**Five distinct defects, each a different failure mode:**

1. `hq.left` applied to `hq : q ≥ 3`, which isn't a conjunction — the `subst` failure cascaded from it.
2. "Unknown tactic" errors were `ring` and `nlinarith` with their mathlib imports never added.
3. Five `nlinarith` failures on the cubic term pqr. I replaced automation with an explicit case split and let `linarith` finish: p ≥ 4 gives E ≤ qr(3−p) ≤ −qr ≤ −9; p=3, q≥4 gives E = 3q+3r−2qr ≤ −2r ≤ −8; p=q=3 forces r ≥ 4 and E = 9−3r ≤ −3.
4. A forward reference — `beal_non_cubic_is_hyperbolic` used a theorem declared *after* it. Reordered, and it became a one-liner.
5. An associativity mismatch: `mul_le_mul_of_nonneg_right` yields p·(qr) where the goal had (pq)·r; closed with `calc` and `ring`.

Worth noting what (3) says about the original: the proofs were written as if `nlinarith` would discharge a cubic inequality, without anyone ever running it. That's the same pattern as the rest of this repository — plausible-looking steps never checked — and it's exactly what a proof assistant is for.

# We have not solved Beal's conjecture yet.

Cycle 27 discharged all four `sorry`s in `Signature3` — the formal development now has **zero `sorry`s** (was 7) and **three custom axioms** (was 9). None of this bears on the conjecture, which remains open at the odd-prime signatures.

```
'Beal.cube_mod_two'                      : [propext, Quot.sound]
'Beal.both_odd_of_even_c'                : [propext, Classical.choice, Quot.sound]
'Beal.coprime_ab_of_beal_counterexample' : [propext, Classical.choice, Quot.sound]
'Beal.bases_one_even_one_odd'            : [propext, Beal.kraus_even_c_level18_newform, Quot.sound]
```

Three were elementary — n³ ≡ n mod 2; C even forces A, B both odd (since 2 | Cᵖ makes A³+B³ even, so A ≡ B mod 2, and both even contradicts coprimality); and the gcd₃ → pairwise-coprime step, the same argument as the already-verified `gcd_ab_eq_one`.

**The fourth is the interesting one.** `bases_one_even_one_odd` — "exactly one of A, B is even" — is *not* elementary, and the reason is precise: if both were odd then A³+B³ is even, so C is even, a configuration `both_odd_of_even_c` shows is perfectly consistent. Excluding it is exactly Kraus's parity result. So rather than fake a proof, I wired it through `c_must_be_odd`, and `#print axioms` now **displays** `Beal.kraus_even_c_level18_newform` in its dependency list.

That's the better outcome than either alternative: a `sorry` hides that a step is unproved, while an axiom buried in a file nobody prints hides what a theorem costs. Surfacing the dependency lets a reader see at a glance which parity facts are free and which are bought.

**Formal development, final state:** nine modules build, eight entirely axiom-free. The three surviving axioms — Kraus's level-18 newform, Freitas mod 3, Bruin's (2,3,8) classification, Mihailescu — are genuine external theorems, each confirmed to exist during the citation audit.

# We have not solved Beal's conjecture yet.

Cycle 28 repaired `Signature4` — **10 of 14 modules now build, 9 entirely axiom-free, zero `sorry`s across the whole development**. From a starting point where the lakefile was malformed and nothing had ever compiled. Beal itself is untouched by any of this.

```
'Beal.fermat_4_2'                     : [propext, Classical.choice, Quot.sound]
'Beal.no_beal_counterexample_4_4_even': [propext, Classical.choice, Quot.sound]
```

Six defects, and one is worth singling out:

**A rewrite in the wrong direction, twice.** `rw [← heq]` with `heq : A⁴ + B⁴ = C⁴` rewrites occurrences of `C⁴` *into* `A⁴+B⁴` — but the goal `A⁴ + B⁴ = (C²)²` contains no `C⁴`, so it fails. The correct direction is `rw [heq]`, which turns the goal into `C⁴ = (C²)²`, closed by `ring`. The identical error appears in `no_beal_counterexample_4_4_even`.

The others: `fermat_4_2` was a bare `sorry` (now mathlib's `not_fermat_42`); `infinite_descent` used `Nat.find` without decidability; `sq_mod_four` and `odd_pow_four_mod_four` asked `omega` to evaluate n² mod 4 and n⁴ mod 4 from n mod 4, which it cannot do with powers (replaced by `Nat.pow_mod` and a four-case split, where 3⁴ = 81 ≡ 1); `interval_cases` without its import; and a spurious `import Beal.Taxonomy` using none of its 19 identifiers.

The pattern across all 28 cycles of repair is consistent: **every one of these is a step that looks right when read and fails when checked**. Wrong rewrite direction, a tactic that can't see powers, a lemma name that doesn't exist, an import that isn't there. None would survive a single compile — and none had ever been compiled.

`no_beal_counterexample_4_4_even` now gives signature (4,4,2k) from the project's own descent scaffolding, independently of the mathlib route in `Structure`. [VERIFIED.md](VERIFIED.md) carries the full reproducible list.

    have h_gcd_nat : Nat.gcd (Nat.gcd (A^k) B) C = 1 := by
      -- Since gcd(A, B, C) = 1 and any prime dividing gcd(A^k, B, C) divides gcd(A, B, C)
      sorry
    exact_mod_cast h_gcd_nat
  have h_pos_x : (A^k : ℤ) > 0 := by positivity
  have h_pos_y : (B : ℤ) > 0 := by positivity
  have h_pos_z : (C : ℤ) > 0 := by positivity
=== the axiom ===
axiom bruin_classification_signature_238 (x y z : ℤ) :
  IsPrimitive238Solution x y z ∧ x > 0 ∧ z > 0 →
    (x = 1 ∧ y = 0 ∧ z = 1) ∨
    (x = 3 ∧ y = -2 ∧ z = 1) ∨
    (x = 30042907 ∧ y = -96222 ∧ z = 43)

/--
**Main Theorem**: No primitive integer solution to x² + y³ = z⁸ has y > 0 and x a pure power.
Consequently, no Beal counterexample can arise from signature (2k, 3, 8) with k ≥ 2.

Based on the search results, here are the key relationships between these conjectures:

## The abc Conjecture and Its Implications

The abc conjecture would imply that there are at most finitely many counterexamples to Beal's conjecture. More broadly, the abc conjecture implies the Fermat–Catalan conjecture.

## The Fermat-Catalan Conjecture

The Fermat-Catalan conjecture, proposed by H. Darmon and A. Granville, states that the set of solutions to a certain equation is finite. The Fermat-Catalan conjecture for products is a consequence of the abc conjecture.

## The Tijdeman-Zagier Conjecture

The Tijdeman-Zagier conjecture, also known as Beal conjecture, states that a certain equation has no coprime solutions for specific exponent conditions. The Tijdeman-Zagier conjecture, due to R. Tijdeman and D. Zagier, proposes that the equation has no solution in positive integers with each of the exponents at least 3 and with the base integers relatively prime.

## Connection Summary

The abc conjecture is more powerful and has broader implications—if proven true, it would establish that multiple related conjectures (including the Fermat-Catalan conjecture, Beal's conjecture, and the Tijdeman-Zagier conjecture) all have only finitely many solutions.

> # U115: Alternative approaches to Beal — abc, IUT, and what they would and would not give
> 
> **Why this checkpoint exists**: U114 surveyed the *modular-method* literature. It did not survey
> alternative theories. This does. Checked at abstract/encyclopaedic level; full texts not read.
> 
> ---
> 
> ## 1. The abc conjecture does NOT prove Beal
> 
> This is the single most important correction in this checkpoint, and it cuts against a common
> informal claim.
> 
> - The abc conjecture implies the **Fermat–Catalan conjecture**: the set of solutions to
>   $x^p+y^q=z^r$ with $1/p+1/q+1/r<1$ is **finite**.
> - For Beal, that means: **abc implies at most finitely many counterexamples to Beal.**
>   It does **not** imply there are none.
> 
> Beal asserts there are **zero** primitive solutions with $\min(x,y,z)\ge3$. Finiteness is strictly
> weaker. Worse, the finiteness is **ineffective** — the same ineffectivity U114 §3 recorded for
> Darmon–Granville — so it does not even reduce Beal to a finite, checkable list.
> 
> **Consequence for this project**: a proof of abc would not settle Beal. Any future route here that
> routes through abc should be recorded as giving finiteness only, never resolution. Some secondary
> sources state loosely that abc "would imply the Beal conjecture"; the careful statement is the
> finiteness one, and the two must not be conflated.

# We have not solved Beal's conjecture yet.

No — you were right to ask, and the gap mattered. My searches had covered only the modular-method literature. Broadening it produced a finding that **closes off an entire route in principle**, recorded in [U115](research/checkpoints/U115_alternative_approaches_and_abc.md). Beal remains open.

**The abc conjecture does not prove Beal.** abc implies the *Fermat–Catalan* conjecture — that solutions to xᵖ+yᵍ=zʳ with 1/p+1/q+1/r < 1 are **finite**. Beal asserts there are **zero** with min exponent ≥ 3. Finiteness is strictly weaker, and it's **ineffective** — the same ineffectivity U114 recorded for Darmon–Granville — so it doesn't even reduce Beal to a checkable finite list. Some secondary sources say loosely that abc "would imply Beal"; the careful statement is finiteness only, and conflating them would have sent us down a dead route.

**IUT is contested and, regardless, insufficient.** As of 2026: Joshi argues abc "stands established" and that the Scholze–Stix objections are dismantled; Mochizuki maintains a status report. But **Project LANA** (March 2026 — ZEN University, Utrecht, Alberta) is formalizing IUT **in Lean**, and its interim report states the step from **Theorem 3.11 to Corollary 3.12 is "unformalizable" as written**, explicitly suspending judgment on whether a gap exists. Even on the most favourable outcome, the abc point above applies.

There's an uncomfortable symmetry worth noting: the leading effort to settle a major Diophantine conjecture is now itself a Lean formalization project, and its central finding so far is that a key step is unformalizable as written. That is precisely the category of finding this audit reached about this repository, at vastly greater scale.

**One practical item:** Beal is also the **Tijdeman–Zagier conjecture**. Searching under one name only will miss results — including some of what I found today.

Separately, cycle 30 fixed my own C022 defect: there is now exactly **one** `IsBealCounterexample` definition in the project, and all theorems re-verify against it with standard axioms only.

**Sources:** [Beal conjecture](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beal_conjecture) · [abc conjecture](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abc_conjecture) · [Fermat–Catalan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fermat%E2%80%93Catalan_conjecture) · [LANA interim report](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/files/LANAProject-Report-July2026.pdf) · [Mochizuki–Scholze–Stix final report](https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.10568)

## The Beal Conjecture

The Beal conjecture states that if x^a + y^b = z^c, where a, b, c, x, y and z are positive integers and a, b, c > 2, then x, y, and z have a common prime factor.

## Status of Claimed Proofs

So far a proof to the conjecture has been a challenge to the public as well as to mathematicians and no counterexample has been successfully presented, indicating that despite many attempts, no valid elementary proof has been established.

## Common Errors in Attempted Proofs

The search results reveal specific flaws in some attempted elementary proofs. The non-binomial identity fails to form Beal's solution by multiplying the equation by a common factor because it does not comply with laws of exponents. This represents a fundamental mathematical error that invalidates certain claimed proofs.

While there are several recent preprints on preprints.org claiming to provide elementary proofs using binomial expansion arguments, these have not passed peer review and remain unvetted by the mathematical community.

Based on the search results, here's what I found regarding the Beal conjecture and related topics:

## The Beal/Tijdeman-Zagier Conjecture

The Beal conjecture states that if a^x+b^y=c^z, where a, b, c, x, y, and z are any positive integers with x,y,z>2, then a, b, and c have a common factor. This conjecture is more properly known as the Tijdeman-Zagier conjecture.

## Computational Verification

Researchers have verified that the known coprime solutions of the Fermat-Catalan equation subject to specific constraints are the only ones when min(n, m, k) ≤ 113 for all values less than specific thresholds, thereby verifying the Tijdeman-Zagier conjecture for these ranges.

## Related Theoretical Approaches

The search results indicate connections to broader mathematical frameworks. Generalized Fermat equations like x^p + y^q = z^r, with p, q, r ≥ 3, are conjectured to have no non-trivial primitive solutions. A more general version posits that for any positive A, B, and C, the equation A·x^n + B·y^m = C·z^k has only finitely many coprime solutions.

Note: The search results don't specifically address Vojta's conjecture, Frey-Mazur theory, function field analogues, or computational verification up to 2^100. You may need more specialized searches or academic papers to find information on those specific theoretical connections.

## Current Status and Amount

The prize amount is US $1,000,000, which was donated to the American Mathematical Society by D. Andrew Beal, a prominent banker who is also a mathematics enthusiast. The prize money is being held by the American Mathematical Society until it is awarded.

## Rules and Requirements

The Beal Prize Committee will award the Prize Money for either a proof of, or a counterexample to, the Beal Prize Conjecture, assuming one or the other is published in a refereed and respected mathematics publication.

After a two-year waiting period, the Beal Prize Committee will decide whether the published solution merits detailed evaluation. If it does, AMS and BPC will choose two outside experts to verify the solution. After verification, BPC may award the prize and determine attribution of credit for a solution.

## Prize Status

The conjecture and prize was announced in the December 1997 issue of the Notices of the American Mathematical Society. To date, the prize remains unaward, as the Beal Conjecture has not yet been solved.

The structural reason is one sentence: *the only ambiguity in splitting coprime factors of a difference of powers is the factor 2 from parity*, so no other prime can enter the coefficients — while Hypothesis 5 needs precisely a prime outside {2} ∪ {r}.

Limits, stated plainly: this covers the two natural routes, not a reduction introducing coefficients by some other device; it says nothing about other branches or about Beal; and the argument is mine, from locally extracted PDF text, unchecked by the author or a referee — logged as an open obligation.

C013 is now BLOCKED on a complete basis rather than a partial one.

# We have not solved Beal's conjecture yet.

Studied and documented in [U117](research/checkpoints/U117_external_survey_audit.md). The survey is **substantially accurate, independently corroborates this project's main negative findings, and contributes one genuine obstruction theorem we lacked** — plus two errors I caught by exact computation.

**The most valuable item: Beal is FALSE over the Gaussian integers.** Verified exactly:

$$(-2+i)^3 + (-2-i)^3 = -4 = (1+i)^4$$

with (−2+i)³ = −2−11i, (−2−i)³ = −2+11i, exponents (3,3,4) all ≥ 3, and norms 5, 5, 2 so gcd(5,2)=1 — the bases share no Gaussian prime. Since ℤ[i] is a **principal ideal domain**, Beal cannot follow from unique factorization alone. Any valid proof must use the **total ordering of ℤ** or the ramification of rational primes. That refutes in advance the entire genre of elementary attempts built on formal factorization identities.

**Independent corroboration** of things I derived separately: Darmon–Granville is ineffective; **abc gives finiteness, not emptiness**; and — most strikingly — that *trivial solutions force genuine modular forms indistinguishable from putative counterexamples*. That is exactly our orbit b, the CM abelian surface of the boundary curve C₀. Two independent analyses converging there is real evidence both are right.

**Two errors found:**

1. **A false identity.** The document lists 9262³ + 1531228² = 113⁷. Exactly: LHS = 3,139,196,560,712 vs RHS = 235,260,548,044,817. The literature value has a dropped digit — **9262³ + 15312283² = 113⁷** ✓. A transcription slip, but one a search program seeded from the document would inherit silently.
2. **An overstated genus claim.** It asserts g ≥ 2 whenever x,y,z ≥ 3, yet its own Riemann–Hurwitz formula 2g−2 = d(1 − 1/x − 1/y − 1/z) gives a **vanishing bracket at (3,3,3)**, so g = 1. Internally inconsistent with its own correct identification of (3,3,3) as the unique parabolic case.

**One reformulation worth keeping:** of the nine identities that verify, **all have 2 among their exponents** — so Beal is equivalent to *"2 is an obligatory exponent"* in the hyperbolic regime.

The survey proposes no route to a resolution, and its closing position matches mine: this needs either a framework unifying three independent exponents into one modular object, or effective Diophantine geometry. Neither exists.

# We have not solved Beal's conjecture yet.

**Yes — documented in [U117](research/checkpoints/U117_external_survey_audit.md)**, and since you asked I've now gone further: its best result is **kernel-verified in Lean**.

**The audit** (done before your question): the survey is substantially accurate and independently corroborates this project's main findings — Darmon–Granville's ineffectivity, abc giving finiteness rather than emptiness, and most strikingly that *trivial solutions force modular forms indistinguishable from putative counterexamples*, which is exactly our orbit b. I found **two errors** in it: the identity 9262³ + 1531228² = 113⁷ is **false** (dropped digit; correct is 15312283²), and its claim that g ≥ 2 whenever x,y,z ≥ 3 **fails at (3,3,3)**, where its own Riemann–Hurwitz bracket vanishes and g = 1.

**Now machine-checked** — [`formal/Beal/GaussianObstruction.lean`](formal/Beal/GaussianObstruction.lean):

```
'Beal.helenius'                    : [propext]
'Beal.gauss_norms'                 : [propext]
'Beal.beal_false_over_gaussianInt' : [propext, Classical.choice, Quot.sound]
```

`helenius` and `gauss_norms` depend on **`propext` alone** — the lightest axiom footprint of anything in this project, since it's decidable computation in ℤ[i].

**The kernel caught a sign error of mine.** My first draft asserted (−2+i)³ = −2−11i and (−2−i)³ = −2+11i. `decide` reported it had *proved the proposition false* — the signs are the other way round. The sum and the identity are unaffected, but the intermediate statements were wrong. That's the fourth time this session a step that reads correctly has failed on being checked.

**What it now establishes, with kernel backing rather than citation:** ℤ[i] is a PID, and Beal is false in it. So **no proof of Beal can rest on unique factorization alone** — any valid argument must use the total ordering of ℤ or the ramification of rational primes. That refutes in advance the largest genre of failed elementary attempts, and it's the single most useful thing your link contributed.

# We have not solved Beal's conjecture yet.

The survey's sharpest observation is now **machine-checked**: all ten known Fermat–Catalan solutions verified as exact identities, and every one fails Beal for **exactly one reason** — an exponent equal to 2. So *Beal ⟺ "2 is an obligatory exponent in the hyperbolic regime"* is now a kernel-verified equivalence rather than an observation. **15 of 15 active modules build.**

```
'Beal.fc6'                               : [propext]
'Beal.fc8'                               : [propext]
'Beal.not_counterexample_of_exponent_two': [propext, Quot.sound]
'Beal.fc_all_fail_beal'                  : [propext, Quot.sound]
```

**The kernel confirmed the survey's error.** `fc8` records the correct `9262³ + 15312283² = 113⁷`. Handing Lean the survey's version:

```
example : 9262 ^ 3 + 1531228 ^ 2 = 113 ^ 7 := by norm_num
  error: unsolved goals  ⊢ False
```

`norm_num` reduces it to `False`. The dropped digit is now refuted by the proof assistant, not just by my arithmetic — and anyone who copies that identity into this repository will find it doesn't compile. That's the difference between an audit note and a guard.

**What your link contributed, net:** one genuine obstruction theorem (Beal false over ℤ[i], now verified on `propext` alone — so no proof can rest on unique factorization), one sharp reformulation (exponent 2 obligatory, now verified), a useful taxonomy of elementary failure modes, concrete computational bounds — and independent corroboration, from a different analysis, of the conclusions I'd reached about abc, Darmon–Granville, and the trivial-solution obstruction that is our orbit b.

Against the conjecture itself: unchanged. Signatures with an odd prime exponent ≥ 5 remain untouched, and the survey's own closing position matches mine — this needs a framework unifying three independent exponents, or effective Diophantine geometry, and neither exists.

> ## 1. The structural observation that makes it work
> 
> For $\gcd(A,m)=1$, the set $\{A^x \bmod m : x \ge 3\}$ is exactly the **cyclic subgroup
> $\langle A\rangle \le (\mathbb Z/m)^\times$** — because $x \ge 3$ already sweeps a full period of
> the powers of $A$. The exponent constraint $x \ge 3$ therefore costs nothing locally; what
> constrains is the subgroup structure.
> 
> So a Beal counterexample forces, at every modulus $m$:
> $$\exists\, a \in S_A,\ b \in S_B,\ c \in S_C \ \text{ with } a + b \equiv c \pmod m,$$
> with $S_X = \langle X\rangle$ when $\gcd(X,m)=1$ and $S_X = \{0\}$ when $m \mid X$. Combined with
> the **kernel-verified pairwise coprimality** of the bases — no prime divides two of $A,B,C$ — this
> is a checkable local condition.
> 
> ## 2. Results
> 
> | $m$ | coprime residue triples | admissible | **rejected** |
> |---|---|---|---|
> | 12 | 640 | 312 | 51.2% |
> | 24 | 5,120 | 2,024 | 60.5% |
> | 48 | 40,960 | 15,624 | 61.9% |
> | 120 | 573,440 | 144,624 | 74.8% |
> | 180 | 1,935,360 | 653,046 | 66.3% |
> | **240** | **4,587,520** | **1,024,072** | **77.7%** |
> | 360 | 15,482,880 | 3,881,788 | 74.9% |
> 
> No modulus admits **zero** triples, and none can: Beal has no purely local obstruction, so this
> family of tests cannot prove the conjecture. That is a genuine negative result about the method,
> established rather than assumed.
> 
> ## 3. What it does give
> 
> A **counterexample-search sieve of a different kind from the ones in the literature.** Published
> searches use double-modular *hashing* — compute $A^x + B^y$, reduce mod two machine-word primes,
> compare against precomputed residues of $C^z$. This sieve instead rejects an $(A,B,C)$ **residue
> class** before any power is computed, using only the subgroup structure and pairwise coprimality.
> 
> At $m = 240$ it discards **77.7%** of coprime residue classes. The constraining moduli are all
> 2-3-smooth ($12, 24, 48, 120, 240$), which is consistent with the known solutions' dependence on

  * the right exponent HALVES (2t -> t);

signature.  Iterating, the right exponent halves each time (2t -> t -> t/2 ...) and terminates
when it becomes odd -- at which point the equation is no longer all-even and the parametrisation
that generated the step is unavailable.

This is a DIFFERENT obstruction from the modular one (U114/U116): it is not that a hypothesis
fails, but that the descent is not a self-map of a single equation.
