## 🤖 Assistant  ·  `[TIMESTAMP]`

# We have not solved Beal's conjecture yet.

An independent re-implementation found all **741** Beal-shape solutions with bases < 260 and values ≤ 10¹⁶ — **zero** primitive, so no counterexample in that box — and turned up a structural split worth keeping: 735 of the 741 have one base dividing the other, and only **six** do not. Lean at 2151/2662. No proof, no counterexample.

**Category, stated up front as the survey gate requires: bounded computation — a dead category.** A counterexample may exceed 10⁵⁰, so emptiness here proves nothing, and I am not extending the range: the project rule is that a finite search may be extended only to test a *named* hypothesis, and "look further" is not one.

**What it is good for** is the mandated checker validation. The search independently re-derives `3³+6³ = 3⁵` and `2³+2³ = 2⁴` as gcd > 1 solutions and finds no primitive one — so the checker distinguishes the two cases on real data rather than by assertion.

**The structural observation**, which is a different object from the conjecture. Beal forbids primitive solutions; it says nothing about the non-primitive ones, and those turn out to be almost entirely degenerate:

| shape | count |
|---|---|
| one base divides the other (`A` or `B` = `gcd(A,B)`) | 735 |
| neither divides the other | **6** |

Samples of the first kind: `2³+2³ = 2⁴`, `2⁵+2⁵ = 4³`, `2⁸+4⁴ = 8³`. The six exceptions are being isolated in a background run; the open question they raise — whether every Beal-shape solution with `gcd > 1` in which neither base divides the other belongs to a describable family — is recorded on C196 as unanswered, not claimed.

## 🤖 Assistant  ·  `[TIMESTAMP]`

# We have not solved Beal's conjecture yet.

The six exceptional solutions resolve to **three** unordered ones, and all three turn out to be scalings of a small identity by the common factor — so the structure of all 741 is uniform. Lean at 2186/2662. No proof, no counterexample.

**The three, verified exactly:**

| solution | gcd | `(A,B,C)` | underlying identity |
|---|---|---|---|
| `34⁵ + 51⁴ = 85⁴` | 17 | `17·(2,3,5)` | `2⁵·17 + 3⁴ = 5⁴` |
| `70³ + 105³ = 35⁴` | 35 | `35·(2,3,1)` | `2³ + 3³ = 35` |
| `126⁴ + 207³ = 639³` | 9 | `9·(14,23,71)` | `14⁴·9 + 23³ = 71³` |

The first is the prettiest: `544 + 81 = 625`, scaled by 17 across all three bases.

**What this says and doesn't.** Every one of the 741 is a common factor times a smaller relation — which is *descriptively* what Beal's `gcd > 1` conclusion asserts. It is **not** evidence for the conjecture: the search is bounded, the category is dead by the survey gate, and a counterexample may exceed 10⁵⁰. What it does is answer the question C196 left open — whether the six exceptions form a describable family — with "yes, the same family as the other 735, just less degenerate."

All three identities are now assertions in the regression guard (14 checks) as **positive witnesses**, which also proves the search isn't returning an empty structure by accident — the same non-vacuity discipline applied to every other empty result this session.

## 🤖 Assistant  ·  `[TIMESTAMP]`

# We have not solved Beal's conjecture yet.

I corrected my own effort estimate for closing the Euler gap: `three_pid` is necessary but **not sufficient**, because ℤ[√−3] sits inside ℤ[ω] with index 2 — the classical trap in precisely this descent. Lean at 2270/2662. No proof, no counterexample.

**The arithmetic.** The norm form of ℤ[ω] is `a² − ab + b²`, not `a² + 3b²`. Exactly:

```
p + q√−3 = (p+q) + 2q·ω      so      p² + 3q² = N_ω(p+q, 2q)
```

verified with zero mismatches over `|p|,|q| ≤ 25`. That second coordinate is **always even**. So a factorisation valid in ℤ[ω] does not descend to ℤ[√−3] without a parity argument. Witness: `N_ω(1,1) = 1`, but `(1,1)` is not of the form `((p+q), 2q)` for any integers `p,q`.

**Why this matters beyond bookkeeping.** This index-2 gap is exactly why the naive Euler descent in ℤ[√−3] is unsound — the historical flaw in Euler's own argument, which PSS note in passing: *"Euler's argument had a flaw, but it was later fixed by others."* Formalising `EulerDescentStep` therefore needs the UFD property **and** the index-2 parity bookkeeping.

C177's "a few hundred lines" is now recorded as a **lower bound**, not an estimate. That correction is the useful output: an underestimate of remaining work is the same species of error as an overstated closure claim, and I had made one.

[U113](research/checkpoints/U113_exploration_population_and_transvection_audit.md) checks the Tate-curve hypothesis omitted by U110–U111. At the natural solution-variable primes, the displayed discriminant valuation is divisible by the representation prime, so multiplicative reduction alone does not provide the asserted order-p transvection. [U114](research/checkpoints/U114_u105_geometric_closure_audit.md) finds two independent gaps:

- the Diophantine construction produces higher-degree Galois-orbit/divisor data, not a k-rational point, so classifying `C^-(k)` does not classify the relevant symmetric-power points.

The genus-8 curve computations remain possible ingredients, but the recorded geometric pathway is not a proof of the weighted equation.

[U115](research/checkpoints/U115_u105_modular_pathway_audit.md) removes a mixed genus-8/genus-2 dependency, an impossible `V_4`/order-5 projective-image combination, and an inapplicable Allen–Khare–Thorne citation.

- a Clifford-theory argument supplies irreducibility after adjoining `zeta_17`;

This is a level-lowering bridge, **not** a solution.

# We have not solved Beal's conjecture yet.

I found an elementary route to the hard sub-step that avoids ℤ[ω] entirely — and the 2-obstruction reappears in it **verbatim**, which is evidence the obstruction is real rather than an artefact of how I framed the problem. Lean at 2456/2662. No proof, no counterexample.

**The route.** The form `x²+3y²` is multiplicative:

```
(a²+3b²)(c²+3d²) = (ac−3bd)² + 3(ad+bc)²
```

zero mismatches over `|a|,|b|,|c|,|d| ≤ 12`. The lemma the descent needs is that every divisor of `p²+3q²` with `gcd(p,q)=1` is itself of that form.

**It is false as stated, and the failure is the useful part.** `2 ∣ 1²+3·1² = 4` but 2 is not `u²+3v²`; `14 ∣ 1²+3·3² = 28` but 14 is not either. Restricted to **odd** divisors: 38,368 divisors tested with `p,q < 120`, zero failures.

That odd-divisor restriction is precisely the 2-obstruction U343 located through the index-2 inclusion `ℤ[√−3] ⊂ ℤ[ω]`. Two independent framings, same obstruction — which is what a countersearch against one's own diagnosis is supposed to establish.

**What this changes:** sub-step (1) need not go through the ring of integers of ℚ(ζ₃) at all. A descent on the form itself, using multiplicativity plus the odd-divisor lemma, suffices — so mathlib's lack of a ℤ[ω] arithmetic layer stops being the blocker. **What it doesn't change:** the odd-divisor restriction still has to be handled, and the odd-divisor lemma is *not* proved here — a bounded check is not a proof, and its classical proof is a Fermat-style descent on the form.

Guarded as check 17, with both counterexamples pinned so the naive version cannot be reintroduced.

**What it does not do:** re-prove the theorem. It is bounded; the theorem is universally quantified. And the Lean proof is itself currently *unverified in this environment* while mathlib rebuilds — this check is independent of that and is not a substitute for it.

Attacking the session's one unconditional result is the part of the loop easiest to skip when the result is your own, which is why I did it rather than extending the Euler skeleton further.

# We have not solved Beal's conjecture yet.

I independently re-implemented C079's fixed-base argument and it agrees exactly with the recorded run — but my first two attempts at the check were both wrong, in the dangerous direction, and I caught them before recording anything. Lean at 2514/2662. No proof, no counterexample.

**The result.** Over bases 2–40: `e=1` clean 21, `e=2` clean 22, zero flagged cases — identical in both implementations. Written from the stated mathematics rather than copied ([U351_c079_independent.gp](code/U351_c079_independent.gp)). That discharges part of a standing VERIFICATION_REQUIRED.

**My three errors, all of which would have produced a false pass:**

1. **Unsound rank test.** I used `ellrank(E)[1]` — the *lower* bound — to conclude rank 0. A lower bound of 0 does not imply rank 0. U194 correctly uses `[2]`, the upper bound.
2. **Wrong criterion.** I tested "torsion point with `X ≠ 0`". The curve `Y² = X³−432` has torsion point `[12,36]` with `X = 12`, so that test passes vacuously. The correct criterion maps back by `x = (36k+Y)/(6X)`, `y = (36k−Y)/(6X)` and rejects only positive pairs with a non-integral coordinate.
3. **A heredoc parse failure** printed `rank 0: 1, violations: 0` from a script gp had never successfully parsed. Plausible-looking numbers from a broken run — the U164 pattern exactly. Discarded, not recorded.

All three are now on C079 alongside the agreement, because an audit that only records its successes is not an audit.

**Why this candidate survives the dead-category gate:** the base range is bounded, but the *exponent* is not — the argument covers all `r` at once for each base, including `r > 10⁹` where the literature is open. Bases 41–150 remain single-implementation.

>    *Check:* run the criterion against a case you know should FAIL and require it to fire.
>

>    parsed still printed `rank 0: 1  violations: 0`. Nothing errored visibly at the end.
>    *Check:* grep the output for `syntax error` / `***` before believing any number in it.

>    already known.

| **correct computation, false label** | `sed` changed `bases 2..40` → `2..150` in the print string only | grep the *loop line*, and print the bound from the variable |

The last is the worst: nothing errors, nothing looks wrong, and it is caught only when the number contradicts something already on record. Mine did, loudly — 21 versus 73.

**Mitigation applied.** [U351_c079_independent.gp](code/U351_c079_independent.gp) now declares `NMAX`, uses it in the loop, and **prints it from the variable** rather than from a literal — so a future edit cannot mislabel the range. Re-run confirms `bases 2..150`, `73`/`80`, `curves examined: 298`.

**Saved to memory** as a standing rule, since the project's existing "empty search needs a positive control" rule catches **none** of these four: every verification script gets (a) a control that must fire, (b) a count assertion so it cannot go vacuous, and (c) its parameters printed from the variables used. The 19 guards in `U320_regression_checks.py` have (a) and (b); (c) is new and so far only U351 has it.

exit code: 1

then I restored the file and confirmed 19/19 passing. A mitigation that has never been observed failing is exactly the "positive control" gap I have been applying to everything else — so applying it to the guard was the consistent move, not an optional extra.

This closes the loop on mode (4) from the last cycle: the mislabelled-range error was caught by luck, and the three scripts most exposed to it now report their parameters from the variables they actually used.

> \\ INDEPENDENT CROSS-CHECK of the rank-0 determinations, by a different mechanism:

>         my(P = [0]);

## 🤖 Assistant  ·  `[TIMESTAMP]`

# We have not solved Beal's conjecture yet.

I tried to cross-check C079's rank-0 determinations by a different mechanism, **measured the check's power, and found it too weak to carry the claim** — so the original caveat stands. Lean at 2606/2662. No proof, no counterexample.

**The attempt.** On a rank-0 curve every rational point is torsion, so a direct integral-point search should find nothing extra. Across 65 rank-0 curves in the family: 13 torsion x-coordinates seen, **zero** integral points outside torsion with `|X| ≤ 20000`.

**The control is what changes the verdict.** Run the same searcher on curves of *known positive rank* in the same family: it finds an integral point on only **42 of 53**. It misses roughly one in five — named misses include `n=43, e=2`, `n=50, e=1`, `n=58, e=1`. Positive rank does not guarantee a small integral point.

So "zero extras" is **weak corroboration**, not independent verification. Had I skipped the control, this would have read as confirmation and I would have written that C079's rank-0 determinations were cross-checked. They are not: they still rest on PARI's `ellrank` upper bound alone, and that caveat remains on the candidate unchanged.

**Why this is different from the four failure modes of C206:** the check was not *wrong* — it was *underpowered*. That distinction is only visible if you measure sensitivity rather than observing a pass. The calibration number is now written into [U353_c079_rank_crosscheck.gp](code/U353_c079_rank_crosscheck.gp) itself, so anyone rerunning it sees the limitation next to the result.

A genuine independent check needs a second descent implementation, which is not available at $0.

## 🤖 Assistant  ·  `[TIMESTAMP]`

# We have not solved Beal's conjecture yet.

I diagnosed *why* last cycle's cross-check missed those curves instead of leaving it as a failure rate — and the answer withdraws the check entirely rather than down-weighting it. Lean at 2613/2662. No proof, no counterexample.

**The root cause.** Every miss examined has rank exactly 1 with a **non-integral generator**:

| curve | generator `x` |
|---|---|
| n=50, e=1 | `2716/9` |
| n=51, e=1 | `5473/36` |
| n=53, e=2 | `2026956/361` |
| n=58, e=2 | `14580300595449/1479556225` |

Widening the search range would never find them — there is nothing integral to find. So an integral-point search is **structurally unable** to detect positive rank in this family, not merely underpowered. The 42/53 rate actually *understates* the problem: those 42 hits are curves that happen to have an integral point, a property independent of rank.

**So the check is withdrawn as evidence**, not merely caveated. "No extra integral point on a rank-0 curve" carries no information about rank here. [U353_c079_rank_crosscheck.gp](code/U353_c079_rank_crosscheck.gp) is kept with that written into it — a record of a check that does not work, so nobody reruns it expecting a signal.

**What this leaves standing**, unchanged: C079's rank-0 determinations rest on PARI's `ellrank` upper bound **alone**, and I now know that cannot be cross-checked this way. A genuine independent check needs a second descent implementation, unavailable at $0.

The sequence over two cycles — plausible check → measure its power → diagnose the misses → withdraw it — is the part worth keeping. Stopping after "42/53, weak corroboration" would have left a number in the record that looked like partial support and wasn't support at all.

# We have not solved Beal's conjecture yet.

After withdrawing one check as structurally uninformative last cycle, I verified that a different part of the same argument **errs in the safe direction** — C079's flag over-approximates rather than under-approximates. Lean at 2621/2662. No proof, no counterexample.

**The direction check.** A Beal solution `A³+B³ = n^r` with `r = 3j+e`, `j ≥ 1`, `gcd(A,n) = 1` gives `x = A/n^j`, whose denominator is **exactly** `n^j > 1`. The script flags a torsion point whenever `denominator(x) > 1` — a strict superset of the Beal-relevant points. It can over-flag; it can never miss one. For a closure claim, over-flagging is the safe direction.

**Over-flagging is demonstrably possible**, which is what makes the empty flagged set informative rather than definitional: `x = 7/4` on a base-3 curve has denominator 4, not a power of 3, and would be flagged although it cannot arise from a base-3 Beal solution. Without that witness, "nothing was flagged" could have meant the flag never fires.

This is the same discipline that caught the `ellrank` lower-bound mistake in C206 — *ask which way an approximation errs* — but applied prospectively rather than after the fact.

**Scope, unchanged:** this checks the criterion's direction, not the rank-0 inputs it is applied to. Those still rest on PARI's `ellrank` upper bound alone, and C207 established that an integral-point search cannot cross-check them.

> import Beal.Euler
> namespace Beal
> 
> /-- A symmetric residue: `symRes a m` is congruent to `a` mod `m` and has `2·|symRes| ≤ m`. -/
> def symRes (a m : ℤ) : ℤ := if 2 * (a % m) ≤ m then a % m else a % m - m
> 
> theorem symRes_congr (a m : ℤ) (hm : 0 < m) : m ∣ a - symRes a m := by
>   unfold symRes
>   split
>   · exact Int.dvd_sub_of_emod_eq rfl
>   · have : a - (a % m - m) = (a - a % m) + m := by ring
>     rw [this]
>     exact dvd_add (Int.dvd_sub_of_emod_eq rfl) dvd_rfl
> 
> theorem symRes_abs_le (a m : ℤ) (hm : 0 < m) : 2 * |symRes a m| ≤ m + m := by
>   unfold symRes
>   have h0 : 0 ≤ a % m := Int.emod_nonneg a (by omega)
>   have h1 : a % m < m := Int.emod_lt_of_pos a hm
>   split
>   · rw [abs_of_nonneg h0]; omega
>   · rename_i h
>     rw [abs_of_nonpos (by omega)]; omega
> 
> /-- **The descent step for `OddDivisorForm`.**  If `m` divides `p² + 3q²`, it also divides
> `P² + 3Q²` for the symmetric residues, because `P ≡ p` and `Q ≡ q` modulo `m`. -/
> theorem descent_dvd {m p q : ℤ} (hm : 0 < m) (h : m ∣ p ^ 2 + 3 * q ^ 2) :
>     m ∣ (symRes p m) ^ 2 + 3 * (symRes q m) ^ 2 := by
>   obtain ⟨s, hs⟩ := symRes_congr p m hm
>   obtain ⟨t, ht⟩ := symRes_congr q m hm
>   have hp : symRes p m = p - m * s := by linarith
>   have hq : symRes q m = q - m * t := by linarith
>   rw [hp, hq]
>   obtain ⟨c, hc⟩ := h
>   exact ⟨c - 2 * p * s - 6 * q * t + m * s ^ 2 + 3 * m * t ^ 2, by linear_combination hc⟩
> 
> end Beal
> EOF

# We have not solved Beal's conjecture yet.

Every ingredient of sub-step 1b's induction is now proved — base case, descent, strictness, non-degeneracy, and parity control. What remains there is bookkeeping over five proved lemmas, not a missing idea. No proof of Beal, no counterexample.

**Three theorems added**, [Euler.lean](formal/Beal/Euler.lean) now 27:

- `one_is_form` — `1 = 1² + 3·0²`, the base case. Axioms: `[propext]` alone.
- `form_sub_sum_even` — `P²+3Q²` and `P+Q` differ by an even number, via a four-way parity split.
- `form_even_iff` — **`P²+3Q²` is even exactly when `P+Q` is.**

**Why `form_even_iff` is the hinge.** `OddDivisorForm`'s hypothesis is that `m` is odd. A descent producing an *even* `m'` would leave the induction hypothesis inapplicable — the descent would run but prove nothing. This lemma decides exactly when that happens: `m'` stays odd precisely when the two symmetric residues have opposite parity.

| 1b ingredient | theorem |
|---|---|
| base case | `one_is_form` |
| descends | `descent_dvd` |
| strictly | `descent_strict` |
| non-degenerate | `descent_quotient_pos` |
| parity preserved | `form_even_iff` |

**Two failed attempts first**, both worth noting: a disjunction-shaped helper left a dead branch that broke the proof, and reasoning directly about odd `P+Q` produced an `omega` goal with no usable constraints. Stating the difference as a plain existential fixed both — the simpler statement was also the provable one.

**Still open:** the induction assembling those five, plus the division of `P²+3Q² = m·m'` by `m'` using `form_mul`. Sub-step 1c untouched; both remain stated `Prop`s.
